name: memx (Rust memchr, memmem, memcmp, memcpy, memset)
baseline: libc memchr, memmem, memcmp, memcpy and memset as shipped by glibc (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and musl (x86_64-unknown-linux-musl), called through the libc crate; the same bench also lists Rust std equivalents and the memchr crate
workload: Per-function benchmark over an English-text haystack (short) and a Japanese-text haystack (long), run for the gnu and musl targets; the table reports time per benchmark run in microseconds (lower is better), with SSE2 and AVX2 variants of each memx function listed separately.
claimed_speedup: memmem on i5-4570: memx 0.798/1.230 us (gnu en/ja) vs libc 2.173/3.828 us, and 0.794/1.197 us (musl en/ja) vs libc 3.948/7.010 us, i.e. about 2.7x, 3.1x, 5.0x and 5.9x (derived from page data). memchr: memx 4.451/5.402 us vs libc 4.849/5.764 us on glibc (about 1.1x) and 4.426/5.322 us vs libc 8.757/10.205 us on musl (about 2.0x, derived from page data). Not uniformly faster: memcmp, memcpy and memset on glibc are slower than libc in several cells (memcpy gnu:en 7.016 us vs 3.483 us, memset gnu:en 3.388 us vs 2.003 us, memcmp gnu:en 2.828 us vs 1.584 us).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.69.0 (84c898d65 2023-04-16); Cargo.toml [profile.bench] opt-level = 3, codegen-units = 1, lto = true; benchmark harness lives in the xbench workspace member.
hardware: Intel Core i5-4570 @ 3.2 GHz (x86_64 gnu and musl targets); also Intel Q6600 @ 2.40 GHz (x86_64, i686, i586) and an armv7 1.5 GHz device in the memchr table.
tradeoffs: Rust crate (no_std capable); SSE2 and AVX2 kernels on x86 and x86_64 only (a *_basic non-SIMD variant is benchmarked for other targets). A separate crate, memx-cdy (github.com/aki-akaguma/memx-cdy), exposes a C ABI and an LD_PRELOAD shim, but its README gives no numbers of its own. memcmp, memcpy and memset do not beat glibc on the author's Haswell-class machine, so the win is concentrated in memmem and in memchr against musl.
caveats: Hardware is a 2013 desktop CPU and a 2007 Core 2 Quad, with rustc 1.69.0 (2023); results are per-run totals on two author-chosen text corpora whose sizes are not stated in the README. The larger gap on musl likely reflects musl's generic C routines being slower than glibc's tuned ones (inference, not stated by the author). Several functions (memcmp, memcpy, memset) are slower than libc in the gnu columns, so only memmem and memchr are real wins. No modern x86 or aarch64 server numbers.
found_via: WebSearch of crates.io API (q=memcmp, q=memrchr) surfaced the crate; opened github.com/aki-akaguma/memx and docs/README.memchr.md, README.memcmp.md, README.memcpy.md, README.memmem.md, README.memset.md

name: asmlib (abiiranathan): AVX2/BMI2 and NEON assembly libc string and memory routines
language: x86-64 assembly (NASM) with AArch64 assembly and C
baseline: glibc 2.44 memcpy, memset, memcmp, strlen, memchr, strstr, memmem and strcmp (libc routines called through volatile function pointers)
workload: bench/bench.c (make bench) measures nanoseconds per call at several sizes with 20000 iterations per size for memcpy, memset, memcmp, strlen, memchr and strstr against glibc; the README reports the outcome per routine.
claimed_speedup: memchr 'consistently faster (about 1.1-1.2x from 128 bytes up)'; mid/large memcpy, memset and memcmp 'at parity (about 0.95-1.2x)'; memmem 'several times faster than libc's'; strcmp/strncmp 'faster than glibc's two-way strcmp'. Losses stated by the author: strlen about 0.5-0.8x under 64 KiB and strstr about 0.4-0.65x versus glibc.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16.2.1 and Clang 22.1.8; Makefile default CFLAGS ?= -O2 -Wall -Wextra; libc and asmlib entry points held in volatile function pointers so the compiler cannot substitute builtins (docs/BENCHMARKS.md).
hardware: Intel Core i7-10510U (Comet Lake), 4 cores / 8 threads, AVX2 + BMI1 + BMI2 + ERMS + FMA, Linux 7.2.
tradeoffs: x86-64 build resolves each routine through ELF IFUNC to AVX2/BMI code or a portable scalar fallback (works on any x86-64 CPU, but the speedups need AVX2); AArch64 port uses NEON; no libc dependency; exposes an asm_* API in asmlib.h rather than overriding libc symbols; routines are page-boundary safe by design; the repo also bundles arena allocator, malloc, math and printf/scanf replacements that are outside this category.
caveats: Repository is only weeks old (first commit 2026-09-27). docs/BENCHMARKS.md says the memory and string results are 'reported qualitatively' because laptop turbo and thermal state swing absolute numbers, so the ratios above come from the README prose, not a fixed table. Single laptop CPU. glibc keeps an edge on strlen and strstr. Parity results for memcpy, memset and memcmp mean no practical gain there. Already reported by a sibling search under hand-written-asm-kernels.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com only): 'faster than glibc strlen memcpy memcmp strcmp implementation AVX2 NEON README benchmark results'; opened README.md, docs/BENCHMARKS.md and Makefile

name: gofiber/utils v2 simd package (AVX2 Memchr2, Memchr3, Memmem, IsASCII for Go)
baseline: Go standard library byte scans: bytes.Index for Memmem, and the stdlib multi-byte search labelled 'default' in the benchmark for Memchr2 and Memchr3; strings/bytes.IndexByte deliberately excluded because the Go runtime already vectorises it
workload: go test ./simd/ -bench=Benchmark_ -count=1 on linux/amd64 for haystacks of 8 B to 4096 B: Memchr2, Memchr3, MemchrPair, MemchrDigit, MemchrWord, Memmem and ASCII scans, each reported as simd, scalar and default rows in ns/op.
claimed_speedup: Memmem at 4096 B: 38.44 ns (simd) vs 921.5 ns (default bytes.Index), about 24x; at 512 B 10.22 ns vs 119.8 ns, about 11.7x (both derived from page data). Memchr2 at 4096 B: 26.22 ns vs 1572 ns for the default row, about 60x (derived from page data). README text also quotes benchstat -count=10 gains of -35% to -88% ns/op against the portable SWAR path at 32-512 B. Slower at small sizes: Memmem 8 B 4.450 ns vs 3.551 ns default.
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain version not stated; go test ./simd/ -benchmem -run=^$ -bench=Benchmark_ -count=1
hardware: linux/amd64, cpu: AMD EPYC (exact model not stated), 4 threads (-4 suffix); arm64 catalog on Apple M2 Pro for the non-SIMD helpers.
stars_or_usage: 57 stars; used by the Fiber web framework
tradeoffs: AVX2 kernels engage only on amd64 for inputs of 32 bytes or more (simd.MinLen); portable SWAR fallbacks elsewhere; []byte only; no single-byte Memchr because bytes.IndexByte is already vectorised; Memmem delegates to bytes.Index up to 64 bytes and bails to it after a bounded number of failed candidates.
caveats: Baseline is the Go standard library, not glibc or musl. Numbers are one run (-count=1) on an unspecified EPYC model and unstated Go version; benchmark charts tracked per commit live on gofiber.github.io, which is blocked here. The kernels are adapted from the coregx/coregex simd package (MIT) with the listed changes, so the novelty is partly upstream. Small inputs (under 32 bytes, and Memmem up to 64 bytes) are at parity or slightly slower.
found_via: WebFetch github.com/topics/memchr and github.com/gofiber/utils (README simd section, Benchmark_Memchr2 and Benchmark_Memmem rows)

name: go-memset (tmthrgd): Go amd64 assembly memset
baseline: Go's own fill loop (README benchmarks BenchmarkGoSet for non-zero fill and BenchmarkGoZero for the zeroing loop idiom)
workload: memset of 32 B to 512 MB buffers; README lists Memset/GoZero/GoSet benchmark outputs and a benchcmp-style old-vs-new table.
claimed_speedup: Non-zero fill: -63.68% ns/op at 32 B, -91.03% at 128 B, -95.80% at 1k (545 ns to 22.9 ns, about 24x derived from page data), -96.78% at 16k, still -87.62% at 512M. Zeroing (already optimised in Go): +84.26% slower at 32 B, +19.90% slower at 1k, equal at 16k-1M, -15% to -18% at 16M and above.
compiler_and_flags: Go version and flags not stated (go test -bench; test file memset_test.go).
hardware: Not stated; benchmark names carry the -8 suffix (8 threads).
tradeoffs: Go package with a pure-Go fallback (memset_other.go); only the amd64 build uses assembly. Archived read-only by the owner on 2024-12-14 and marked 'Not maintained' in the README.
caveats: Baseline is a Go loop, not libc; the old column is inferred from matching BenchmarkGoSet/BenchmarkGoZero numbers because the README does not label it. Numbers date from the Go 1.x toolchains of 2016-2018 and no CPU model or Go version is given; later Go toolchains may behave differently, especially for zeroing, which the compiler already maps to its own memclr routine. Zeroing is slower than Go's loop for small buffers.

name: memcpy_fast (gamesun): Cortex-M4 word and doubleword memcpy
baseline: the toolchain's standard memcpy on Cortex-M4 (C library not stated)
workload: Copy of a 10240-byte buffer with offsets a, b and c added to the destination, source and length, dest and src 8-byte-aligned arrays; results shown only as an image (memcpy_fast_vs_memcpy.png).
claimed_speedup: 'A 1.3 to 5.2 times faster memcpy, optimizing depends on data blocks alignment on Cortex-M4' (README description; per-case values are only in the PNG).
hardware: Cortex-M4 (part number and clock not stated)
tradeoffs: Plain C: copies with long long (LDRD/STRD) loops when source and destination share 8-byte alignment and with 32-bit long loops otherwise, relying on the compiler's code generation and on Cortex-M4 unaligned LDR/STR support; casts between integer widths without regard to strict aliasing; GPL-3.0 licence blocks use in permissive code; Cortex-M4 only.
caveats: No numeric table, compiler, flags or MCU part in the text; the 1.3-5.2x range cannot be checked and the baseline C library (newlib, vendor libc) is unnamed. Eleven commits in August 2020, no later activity.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com only): 'github memcpy memset strlen optimized assembly faster than newlib cycles benchmark Cortex-M ...'

name: memcpy_threaded / memset_threaded (Carandiru0 mem.h gist)
baseline: single-threaded compiler-intrinsic memcpy and memset on Windows (MSVC-style code); a multithreaded intrinsic version is the middle row
workload: Large-buffer copy and fill using AVX/SSE intrinsics, Intel TBB parallel_for and PrefetchVirtualMemory; header comments quote GB/s for single-thread intrinsic, multithreaded intrinsic and the threaded routine.
claimed_speedup: 'intrinsic memcpy (single threaded) at 22 GB/s', 'intrinsic memcpy (multithreaded) at 29 GB/s', '___memcpy_threaded at 33.3 GB/s (memory bandwidth is saturated)'; memset_threaded also 33.3 GB/s (write bandwidth). That is about 1.5x over the single-threaded intrinsic (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Windows and MSVC specific (__declspec, #pragma loop, PrefetchVirtualMemory) and needs Intel TBB; threads only pay off once a single core cannot saturate memory bandwidth; the NonCommercial-ShareAlike licence is not OSI-approved.
caveats: Numbers are code comments from the author with no CPU, compiler or flags and no harness; baseline is the author's own intrinsic memcpy, not the CRT memcpy. The '16x faster' line about SSE stores over rep stosb is quoted from a Microsoft blog, not measured. Last gist activity 2025-06-10; code dated 2022.
found_via: WebSearch result (github.com only) listing 'optimized memcpy_threaded, memset_threaded' gist
